doc.title: David Friesen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2024

title: How Friesen composes: playing time with no changes, and the tune Neves
summary: He describes writing from improvised time playing and finding odd meters like the seven in Neves.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah sometimes it is, you know I’ll take my bass out of the corner of the music room and just play time, no changes. I’ll count off a tempo and I’ll just play time, no changes. I’m improvising. And this has been a process of how I write music — one way that I wrote music — and I would play time, no changes for about 15, 20 minutes and then I wouldn’t listen to it the same day, the next day I would listen to it. You get a little bit more of an objective view that way. And I’d hear a lot of garbage, so I would take out the garbage like I do in my home, we have a trash can, but I’d hear something that I liked and I’d stop the recording, I’d find out what is that. And then I would write a song based on that idea. So that’s one way. Sometimes I’m playing and I’ll hear myself play a certain idea and I’ll follow it through and then another idea may come — like on this tune — play this figure over and over again and then find a line that will work with this, now go to the piano and record it, both parts, because I can hear it a little clearer that way, and all the harmony is right there. So I don’t have one method of writing music. There’s different things. This one I think I was just playing and heard this line — I never think I’m going to write in an odd time, I want to write a tune in, you know, in seven or five. I just write the music and then when I go to put it down I find sometimes to my dismay — oh wow, I’m going to have to learn how to play this.
It’s funny you say that because when I was trying to transcribe the line I was having trouble with where’s one. And —
